To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) GAN training is equivalent to approximate divergence minimization, (2) GAN training can be understood as an instance of the stochastic approximation framework, and (3) the divergence minimized by the GAN training process is a function of the discriminator’s loss function.

1) GAN training can be understood as minimizing a divergence between the data distribution and the model distribution; 2) this divergence can be expressed as a weighted sum of two divergences, one of which corresponds to the Wasserstein-1 metric, while the other is related to the Wasserstein-Kantorovich-Rubinstein (WKR) metric; and 3) the weights depend on the discriminator architecture, and can be estimated by analyzing the discriminator gradients.

(1) the training of GANs with a non-saturating loss function can be interpreted as approximate minimization of the Jensen-Shannon divergence; (2) this divergence can be estimated from the data using the Wasserstein distance; (3) this interpretation provides a principled way of choosing the number of training epochs and the batch size; and (4) this interpretation allows to estimate the quality of the generator from the data, without relying on the discriminator.
